newsitem.title: USA: Resource waste must be tracked, U.S. group says.
newsitem.headline: Resource waste must be tracked, U.S. group says.

text.p: Every American annually uses an average of 84 tonnes of Earth's resources to support his or her lifestyle, the World Resources Institute (WRI) said on Monday.
"This is a lot of stuff that is used to ... support the economy," WRI president Jonathan Lash said, pointing to 43 bags of trash symbolising the material used by each American every day.
The group urged the U.S. government to follow the example of Germany and the Netherlands and begin to assess ecological efficiency as part of the overall picture of the economy.

Policymakers need the statistics to prevent the plundering of the environment rather than having to spend billions of dollars to clean up the environment after the fact, WRI officials said at a news briefing.
The report said Germans and Dutch used the same amount of resources per person as Americans. In contrast, Japanese used only 45 tonnes per person annually, it said.

"(The Japanese) use less energy and they're more efficient in using it," said WRI's Allen Hammond, one of the authors of the report. Japan has far less impact on the environment partly because the country does not depend on coal, he said. Coal mining entails a lot of "hidden" resource use from digging and soil removal, according to the report's measures.
If industrialised countries continue on their current path and developing countries catch up, 50 years from now people will be using five times as much resources, Hammond said.

Resource flows could be cut substantially using existing technology including using more recylable materials and extending the economic lifetime of some commodities, said Albert Adriaanse, another author of the report.
Hammond said by tracking resource use governments could come up with better environmental policies, including taxes to prevent resource waste.
The report was done by WRI, the German Wuppertal Institute, the Netherlands Ministry of Housing, Spatial Planning and Environment and the Japanese National Institute for Environmental Studies.
